requirements.requirement: Install a file-integrity tool (AIDE) on node1, since it was not present and no yum repos were enabled
requirements.summary: node1 had no aide package and no enabled repos (cmd-00f5abf325234d3a, cmd-4ae8fd295d364482). Executor downloaded a matching RHEL7-compatible aide RPM from vault.centos.org and installed it via rpm -ivh, confirmed present afterward (rpm -ql aide).

requirements.requirement: The integrity baseline must cover /etc so later changes to files there can be identified
requirements.summary: aide.conf shows a tree-wide '/etc/ PERMS' rule plus CONTENT_EX (hash+perm) rules for dozens of specific /etc subpaths/files (passwd, shadow, ssh config, sudoers, systemd, etc.), giving broad and specific coverage of /etc.

requirements.requirement: Initialize the baseline database representing the current state of /etc (and other covered paths)
requirements.summary: aide --init built a new database, which was copied to aide.db.gz and activated; a subsequent aide --check against it reported a clean 'All files match AIDE database' result, confirming the baseline reflects current state.

requirements.requirement: Baseline can identify and report later changes to files in /etc
requirements.summary: Appending text to the AIDE-tracked file /etc/issue caused aide --check to exit 4 and report the file changed with differing SHA256 hashes, directly demonstrating detection. After reverting, aide --check returned clean again, showing the baseline remains usable and accurate.

overall_summary: The executor installed AIDE on node1 (which had no aide package or enabled repos) via a manually sourced RHEL7-compatible RPM, initialized and activated a baseline database whose configuration covers /etc broadly (tree-wide PERMS plus CONTENT_EX for many specific config files), and directly demonstrated both a clean baseline state and successful detection of a tracked-file change (/etc/issue), followed by a return to clean. All material task outcomes are satisfied with direct, coherent evidence. Separately, the mandatory node-restart protocol is also well evidenced: healthy pre-restart state, restart acknowledgement, a genuinely different post-restart boot identity, and confirmed post-restart recovery of the same baseline database and clean AIDE check. The main deduction is an unreverted test mutation to /etc/motd left as residue, plus some uncleaned temp files.
limitations: The initial 'package-health' lifecycle check timed out both before and after the task, so no native package-manager consistency signal is available to independently confirm rpm database integrity after the unsigned-RPM install.
The /etc/motd test line added by the executor (cmd-41d843915f8f4d80) was never reverted; no evidence shows it was cleaned up before task completion.

operational_hygiene.summary: Most executor mutations were purposeful and either required (installing aide, building the database) or bounded and reverted (the /etc/issue detection test, reverted by cmd-1449272c1c7c4951; the stale yum lock cleanup in cmd-63ce56afc76a4ae7, which killed an already-gone PID and removed a stale lock file blocking yum). However, cmd-41d843915f8f4d80 appended a test line ('# integrity-baseline-test <date>') to /etc/motd as a detection experiment, discovered it wasn't AIDE-tracked, then moved on to testing /etc/issue instead -- but never reverted the /etc/motd change. This is an unnecessary mutation to a live system file that was left as residue with no task-related purpose. Additionally, several temp artifacts (aide RPM, aide-check-*.log, aide-init.log/pid, reboot.log) were left in /tmp per the after-executor snapshot; these are low-risk but uncleaned byproducts of the work.
